paras: The attempted lynching of Cornelins Hyman took place at Pearlington, Hancock County, Mississippi, on July 30–31, 1900, when armed white men chased and shot at a Black youth accused of attacking an elderly white woman with an ax. He was arrested unharmed the next morning and jailed at Bay St. Louis amid threats of lynching.

According to the Sea Coast Echo, Hyman, a "negro boy" of about 16 to 18, came to Henry Baker's house on Monday afternoon, asked Mrs. Baker for water, then seized an ax and attempted a "criminal assault." She fled screaming, drawing her sons from nearby work.

The sons armed themselves and fired several shots after him, but "none took effect." An organized search went on all night amid "all kinds of talk and threats of lynching" until Constable D. Caddy arrested him at Logtown at 10 o'clock Tuesday morning. Although some feared the constable would be intercepted, Constable John Lafontaine delivered him "without interference" to Sheriff Cazeneuve, who jailed him to await circuit court.
A Corinth weekly reported that he "made a confession" after being run down; the local paper did not mention one. No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

Only two white Mississippi papers carried the case, and no Black-press coverage was found. The Weekly Corinthian ran it first, on August 1, as an unnamed item in its state-news column under "Charged With Attempting Criminal Assault on White Lady." The Sea Coast Echo followed on August 4 with a full story headed "His Neck Narrowly Saved," crediting "cool judgment and a law-abiding people" while calling the youth "old enough to show a criminal beastly instinct." It added that a "neck-tie party would have cut down a bad weed while yet young," but that local citizens had "saved Hancock from disgrace."

The Corinthian placed the assault at Logtown and named one son as the shooter; the Echo, the fuller county-seat account, set it at Pearlington, with Logtown as the place of arrest, and described several armed sons.

bases: Armed white pursuers fired several shots at the fleeing youth and there were 'threats of lynching' and fears the prisoner would be taken from the constable, but he was jailed unharmed, an attempted lynching (A3, A1).

Two separate Mississippi reports, a Corinth state-news brief (A1) and the Bay St. Louis local account (A3), agree on the alleged ax assault on an elderly woman, the shooting at the fleeing youth by her son(s), and his capture the next day, though they differ on place and detail.

accounts.label: Local county-seat paper
accounts.gist: The Sea Coast Echo named Hyman and Mrs. Baker, set the assault at Pearlington, described armed sons firing several shots in an all-night pursuit and lynching threats, and reported his quiet arrest at Logtown and jailing at Bay St. Louis.

accounts.label: State-news brief
accounts.gist: The Weekly Corinthian, without names, set the assault at Logtown, said her son shot at the fleeing youth, and that after a night in the swamps he was run down and 'made a confession'.

framing.detail: The Echo praised the 'law-abiding people' and 'dignity of the law' for avoiding a lynching yet wrote that 'A neck-tie party would have cut down a bad weed while yet young' and called the youth 'old enough to show a criminal beastly instinct'.
The Corinthian ran the case as one line under the subhead 'Charged With Attempting Criminal Assault on White Lady' in its state-news roundup, ending with his reported confession.

versions.value: Pearlington (the Baker house); arrest at Logtown

conflicts.note: The Echo, published at the county seat and giving names and officers, is the more detailed local source; the Corinthian may have conflated the arrest site with the scene.

versions.value: Her sons (plural), armed, plus an organized all-night search
Her son (singular) shot at the fleeing negro

conflicts.note: Only the Corinthian brief reports a confession.

sources.note: Local county-seat account: names Cornelins Hyman and Mrs. Henry Baker; armed sons fired shots in pursuit; arrested at Logtown by Constable D. Caddy; jailed by Sheriff Cazeneuve; lynching threats; paper says 'A neck-tie party would have cut down a bad weed'.
quotes: They fired several shots while in pursuit but none took effect.
There was all kinds of talk and threats of lynching, but a better spirit predominated and he was extraordinarily fortunate in the luck that saved his neck.
It was feared in some quarters at Pearlington that the constable would be intercepted and the prisoner lynched.
A neck-tie party would have cut down a bad weed while yet young, but Pearlington and Logtown citizens did wisely and saved Hancock from disgrace.
